'The cut-off for science is 85,' Kiran said, dropping onto the sofa. 'I got 79 in the pre-boards. It's over, Lokesh bhaiya.'
Lokesh muted the cricket. 'Is it? When are the actual boards?'
'March. But the paper setters, the checking, the cut-off, I can't control any of that.'
'True. So what can you touch today? Not March. Today.'
Kiran was quiet. 'I lost most marks in chemistry equations.'
'Okay. And?'
'I could do ten equations tonight. And ask Farida Ma'am tomorrow which ones I keep getting wrong.'
'That's today's thing. The cut-off is the cut-off.'
Kiran pulled the chemistry book out of the bag. 'And if I still don't make it?'
'Then you'll have done your part, and we'll look at the other streams together. Not your fault either way.'
'Ten equations,' Kiran said. 'Starting now.'

qa.q: What score did Kiran get in the pre-boards?
qa.a: 79 in the pre-boards, while the cut-off for science is 85.

qa.q: How was Kiran feeling when saying 'It's over'?
qa.a: Kiran felt hopeless, focusing only on the cut-off and the checking, which were out of Kiran's hands.

qa.q: What turning point moved Kiran from despair to action?
qa.a: Lokesh's question about what Kiran could touch today led Kiran to one step: ten equations tonight and asking Farida Ma'am which ones go wrong.

qa.q: How might Lokesh bhaiya see the role of an older brother in a moment like this?
qa.a: Lokesh seems to see the role as a steady helper who asks questions rather than lecturing, so Kiran finds the next step and keeps hope without self-blame.

grounding: Shows a teenager asking what can be done today, taking one action, and accepting that the cut-off itself cannot be changed.

passage:
When we moved from Lucknow to Nagpur last June, I spent the first three weeks in my room. 'Farhan, come and eat,' Ammi would call, and I'd say later. I couldn't change Abbu's transfer. I couldn't make my old friends live closer. Every night I scrolled through old photos and felt worse.
Then one evening I made a list on my phone: things I can do this week. It was short. Say hi to one person in class. Call Ayaan on Sunday. Find out if the school has a quiz club.
It did. That's where I met Aadhya, who argues about capital cities like her life depends on it. We came second at the inter-school round in October.
I still miss Lucknow. Some days a lot. But I stopped blaming myself for being lonely, and I stopped waiting for things to fix themselves.

qa.q: What was on the list of things to do that week?
qa.a: Say hi to one person in class, call Ayaan on Sunday, and find out if the school has a quiz club.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling in the first three weeks in Nagpur, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Farhan was sad and lonely; staying in the room, putting off meals and scrolling old photos every night show it.

qa.q: Which choice made the difference for Farhan, and why?
qa.a: Making a short list of small actions within reach, instead of wishing the transfer away, led to the quiz club and a new friend.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see Farhan, the newcomer at the quiz club?
qa.a: Aadhya likely sees a teammate who shares the love of quizzing, not someone lonely, since they came second together in October.

grounding: Shows a teenager who accepts a move they could not change, takes small actions within their control, and keeps hope without blaming themselves.

passage:
Physio room note, Wednesday. Darshan hurt his knee two weeks before the district trials, and this week the doctor said he would miss them. He sat on the bench for a long time, silent. Then he asked me, "Okay. What can I actually do today?" We made a short list: the exercises he's allowed, watching match videos to study positioning, helping coach the juniors on Saturday. He crossed off the first one before he left. He also said, "The trials are gone this year. I can't change that part." He didn't blame himself or anyone. Next step: I will check his list on Friday.
Preeti

qa.q: What will Darshan help with on Saturday?
qa.a: Helping coach the juniors.

qa.q: What might Darshan have been feeling while he sat silent on the bench?
qa.a: He was likely disappointed and upset about missing the trials he'd worked for.

qa.q: Why was Darshan's question a wise one?
qa.a: Asking what he could do today turned helplessness into small actions while accepting the trials were gone.

qa.q: How might Preeti see Darshan by the end of the session?
qa.a: Preeti likely feels hopeful and impressed, seeing him act without blaming anyone.

grounding: Shows a teen asking what is within his control today, taking one action and accepting what can't be changed.

passage:
Sunday night. Mum and Papa told us today they're separating. I cried for an hour in the bathroom, and then I did the thing Maria's mum taught us in Guides: two columns. Things I can't change: their decision, which house we live in, what happened between them. Things I can do today: finish my geography map, call Maria, make sure Chotu eats dinner, tell Papa I love him even though I'm angry. I did three of the four. I haven't told Papa yet. Tomorrow. It still feels like the floor is tilting. But one column is mine, and that helps a little.
Damini

qa.q: How long did Damini cry in the bathroom?
qa.a: For an hour.

qa.q: How is Damini feeling after the news?
qa.a: Damini feels shaken and angry, as if the floor is tilting, but a little steadier after the list.

qa.q: How did the two columns help Damini?
qa.a: They separated what Damini can't change from small actions for today, giving some hope without self-blame.

qa.q: What is it like for Chotu on this day?
qa.a: Chotu, the younger one, is probably confused and upset too, and relies on Damini to make sure dinner happens.

grounding: Illustrates a teen listing what is and isn't within reach after hard news and taking actions for today.

passage:
The hailstorm flattened half of Rajni's family's mustard field two weeks before her board exams. Her father sat silent on the charpai. The house felt heavy.
That night Rajni couldn't study. Her friend Hansa came by with a lantern. "What are you thinking?"
"That I can't fix the field. That maybe nothing I do matters."
Hansa sat down. "What can you do today? Just today."
Rajni thought. "I can't bring the mustard back. But I can finish the history chapter. And I can help Bapu clear the broken stalks in the morning."
She wrote both on the back of her hand in pen. She studied for an hour, then slept.
At dawn she was in the field beside her father, pulling stalks. He didn't say much, but he handed her the water bottle first.

qa.q: What did the hailstorm flatten?
qa.a: Half of Rajni's family's mustard field.

qa.q: How was Rajni feeling the night of the storm?
qa.a: She felt hopeless and heavy, thinking she couldn't fix the field and that nothing she did mattered.

qa.q: What made Rajni's two small actions wise?
qa.a: She accepted she couldn't bring the mustard back, but chose actions within her control that day, the history chapter and helping clear stalks, which kept hope without self-blame.

qa.q: How might Rajni's father feel when she joins him in the field?
qa.a: He was silent and heavy after the storm, but handing her the water bottle first suggests he felt comforted and grateful for her help.

grounding: Shows a teen asking what is within her control after a loss she cannot change, taking one action, and keeping hope without self-blame.
